paragraphs: BLHT is a reinforcement learning algorithm for environments where the learner cannot directly observe everything relevant to its decisions. It uses short-term memory to supplement current observations. This gives the learner a limited history to work with when predicting what it will perceive and what rewards it will receive, rather than treating the present observation as a complete description of the situation.

The algorithm learns a probabilistic model through Bayesian learning. Its predictions can therefore describe uncertainty about future observations and rewards. The authors report that this approach reasonably addresses overfitting and has an efficient implementation. The overfitting claim is qualified: the abstract presents Bayesian learning as a practical response to the problem, rather than a guarantee that overfitting is impossible.

The main theoretical finding concerns convergence of the learned model. BLHT approaches a model providing the most accurate predictions available given its short-term memory. That qualification defines the result: predictive optimality is tied to the information retained in memory, rather than to unrestricted access to the environment's hidden state or entire history.
neurips-1998-a-reinforcement-learning-al.tldr: BLHT uses Bayesian learning and short-term memory to learn optimal predictions of observations and rewards within the information its memory retains.

paragraphs: The paper addresses a mismatch between smooth spatial models and physical fields that contain abrupt changes. Gaussian processes provide useful prior models for spatial data, but their smoothness can be excessive for some applications. Near-surface wind fields illustrate the issue: a front can form a boundary across which the field changes discontinuously.

The proposed method adds a constrained discontinuity to a Gaussian process model. The central modeling idea is to accommodate an abrupt change along a bounding surface within the spatial description. This matters because the boundary is part of the physical structure being represented. A model that smooths across it can fail to express the kind of change the authors want to capture.

The paper also demonstrates inference of the model parameters for wind fields using Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling. This connects the proposed representation to a method for estimating it from data. The contribution is thus both a way to express constrained spatial discontinuities and a demonstrated sampling-based approach to parameter inference in the motivating wind-field setting.
neurips-1998-adding-constrained-disconti.tldr: The paper adds constrained discontinuities to Gaussian process wind-field models and demonstrates parameter inference using MCMC.

paragraphs: The paper develops an algorithm and integrated vision sensor for extracting self-motion information from optical flow, the pattern of apparent motion across an image. It targets a singular point associated with expansion or rotation. Locating this point provides a compact description of motion that can support visual guidance for a moving platform.

The sensor is a fully parallel analog CMOS VLSI array. Each pixel determines the sign of local optical flow, supplying directional information without requiring the full flow magnitude. The array can directly implement the authors' integrative algorithm. Measurements show real-time computation of the singular point with power consumption below 2 milliwatts, linking the method to a concrete low-power hardware implementation.

More general flow fields require additional information about expansion and rotation. The authors show that these quantities can also be computed in real-time hardware using flow signs alone. Together with the singular point's location, these measurements provide the robust self-motion information described in the paper. The contribution combines a compact motion representation with hardware suited to computing it continuously.
neurips-1998-an-integrated-vision-sensor.tldr: A parallel analog vision sensor extracts optical-flow singular points in real time using motion signs and less than 2 milliwatts.

paragraphs: Learning a temporal probabilistic model from partially observed data repeatedly requires inference about hidden quantities. This can be expensive because inference traverses long observation sequences and manipulates data structures that grow exponentially. The paper addresses this computational burden within expectation-maximization, or EM, for temporal Bayesian networks.

The authors use a previously developed approximate monitoring algorithm for EM's forward propagation step and introduce a related approximation for the backward step. They prove error bounds for the combined inference procedure. In a real-world application, EM with this approximate inference runs much faster than EM with exact inference, with almost no loss in learned-model quality. That quality finding is empirical and specific to the reported application.

The paper also considers online learning, where updates can use a limited observation window. It bounds the error introduced by restricting attention to that window and presents an online EM algorithm for dynamic systems. The reported online method learns much faster than standard offline EM. Together, the results connect computational savings to explicit analysis of the approximations involved.
neurips-1998-approximate-learning-of-dyn.tldr: Approximate forward and backward inference makes temporal-model EM faster, with error bounds and little empirical loss in model quality.

paragraphs: The paper examines how object classification depends on the meaning of similarity. A similarity function determines which previously encountered objects should inform the classification of a new one. The authors identify a tension: complex similarities appear necessary for cognitive models and applications, while simpler similarities make established computational approaches easier to use.

Their response is to develop supervised learning methods that accommodate non-metric similarities. One direction concerns parametric classifiers that summarize a category by its mean. The paper discusses how to implement this style of representation when the similarity function does not provide the usual metric setting. This extends a familiar way of representing classes to a broader kind of comparison.

The second direction concerns non-parametric classification through nearest neighbors in non-metric spaces. The paper reviews methods the authors developed for this purpose, with some of that work described more fully elsewhere. The contribution is to show computational ways forward for richer similarity functions. It treats the choice of similarity as a fundamental part of the learning problem, with consequences for both class summaries and example-based decisions.
neurips-1998-classification-in-non-metri.tldr: The paper develops and reviews classification methods that can use complex, non-metric notions of object similarity.

paragraphs: The paper studies classification when objects are described by pairwise proximities rather than explicit feature vectors. This representation records relationships between objects directly. It is more general than starting with Euclidean vectors, since those vectors can produce proximities, while a proximity-based description need not supply such coordinates.

The authors propose two approaches. The first combines a linear embedding with classification, extending the Optimal Hyperplane algorithm to pseudo-Euclidean data. The second applies a linear threshold model directly to proximity values and trains it using Structural Risk Minimization. These offer two routes from relational information to a classifier: construct a suitable representation while learning, or use the measured relationships themselves as the model's inputs.

The paper also explains how distance choices can incorporate prior knowledge and examines how different metrics affect generalization. Applications to protein structures and cat cerebral-cortex data outperform K-nearest-neighbor classification in the reported tests. The findings support learning a classification rule from proximity data, while also showing that the way proximity is defined is a meaningful modeling choice.
neurips-1998-classification-on-pairwise-.tldr: Two classifiers learn directly from pairwise proximities and outperform K-nearest neighbors on the reported biological datasets.

paragraphs: A common way to encode a time series is to split it into short blocks and describe each block with basis functions. The paper identifies an alignment problem: block boundaries need not line up with the signal's underlying events. Its algorithm avoids blocking and instead infers where basis functions should occur in time.

The functions can span arbitrary durations and need not be orthogonal. This flexibility allows the representation to capture structure wherever it occurs while preserving the relative timing of events. The authors show that the model is equivalent to a highly overcomplete basis used very sparsely: many possible functions and placements are available, but the representation draws on a small subset.

Finding the representation is nonlinear, yet the authors report that it can be computed efficiently. The formulation also supports existing methods for adapting the basis to data. Applied to speech, it produces a shift-invariant, spike-like representation resembling cochlear-nerve coding. This resemblance is a reported property of the representation, rather than a demonstration that the model explains the biological coding mechanism.
neurips-1998-coding-time-varying-signals.tldr: The algorithm encodes time series with sparsely placed basis functions, preserving event timing without imposing fixed block boundaries.

paragraphs: The paper studies recurrent neural networks whose connections operate at two spatial scales: between nearest neighbors and over longer distances. The relative influence of these interactions can be tuned. This makes competition between local and distant connections an explicit part of the model, allowing the authors to examine how it affects the network's recall behavior.

The authors obtain exact analytical equilibrium solutions for a class of these networks. Their treatment includes both sequential and parallel neuronal dynamics, covering models in which neurons update in sequence as well as models with simultaneous updates. The contribution is an analytical characterization of the modeled behavior, rather than solely observations from numerical runs.

The competition produces coexistence phenomena and abrupt transitions involving recall states, non-recall states, and two-cycles, which alternate between two states. Thus, changing the balance of interactions can change the kind of behavior the network exhibits discontinuously. Within the analyzed model class, the findings connect memory recall and cycling behavior to the interaction between local and long-range connections.
neurips-1998-discontinuous-recall-transi.tldr: Exact analysis shows that competing local and long-range connections can induce coexistence and abrupt transitions among recall, cycling, and non-recall states.

paragraphs: Dynamic trees are image models that place a prior distribution over many possible tree structures. Each candidate structure is itself a tree-structured belief network. The model therefore includes uncertainty about the tree used to represent an image, giving it structural flexibility beyond a single fixed arrangement of connections.

The authors compare this approach with a fixed, balanced tree-structured belief network. Their experiments show that dynamic trees can generate images with less blockiness and have better translation-invariance properties. In plain language, the reported results suggest that allowing the structure to vary reduces visible artifacts associated with the fixed tree and improves how the model handles changes in image position.

The paper also investigates how to find useful tree structures. Simulated annealing is shown to locate trees with high posterior probability, meaning structures favored after the image evidence is taken into account. This provides an effective search method for the proposed model in the reported experiments. The combined contribution is a flexible family of image representations and evidence that useful members of that family can be found.
neurips-1998-dts-dynamic-trees-0c081c87e.tldr: Dynamic trees model images using many possible tree structures, producing less blocky images and better translation invariance in experiments.

paragraphs: The paper addresses model selection in support vector machines through the kernel parameter. This parameter controls the complexity of the learned hypothesis, so choosing it is part of deciding what kind of model to fit. The usual approach described by the authors uses a validation set to make that choice separately from training.

Their algorithm brings parameter selection into the learning process. It adjusts the kernel dynamically, seeking the parameter that gives the best possible upper bound on generalization error. The optimization target is therefore a bound on performance for unseen data. Improving this bound provides a principled selection criterion, although the bound and the actual generalization error are distinct quantities.

The authors report that the method needs no validation set and adds little computational cost. They provide theoretical motivation and experiments supporting the approach's validity. Its significance is the integration of two tasks normally handled separately: learning the classifier and selecting its kernel parameter. The claimed efficiency concerns this integrated procedure, while the theoretical objective explains how it chooses among parameter values.
neurips-1998-dynamically-adapting-kernel.tldr: The method adapts SVM kernels during training to optimize a generalization-error bound without a validation set and with little added computation.

paragraphs: The paper investigates what kind of internal model supports human adaptation to unfamiliar movement dynamics. It compares two adaptive-control architectures: one using only an inverse model, and another combining forward and inverse models. The aim is to distinguish their explanations of learning by comparing their movement patterns with those of human subjects.

The comparison concerns hand-reaching movements in novel force fields. Among the architectures examined, learning a forward model produces key performance characteristics that match human movement kinematics. The inverse-only architecture fails to reproduce those observed patterns, even though it is more stable. This makes the detailed form of the movement an important source of evidence beyond whether a controller remains stable.

The findings support the idea that adapting to novel dynamics involves forming a forward model. The strength of the conclusion comes from the contrast between the tested architectures and the human movement data. It is evidence for a particular account of adaptation in this setting, with the forward-model architecture capturing characteristics that the tested inverse-only alternative does not.
neurips-1998-evidence-for-a-forward-dyna.tldr: Comparisons with human reaching movements support forward-model learning as an account of adaptation to novel force fields.

paragraphs: The paper presents a Bayesian method for retrieving shapes represented as graphs from a large structural database. Matching considers both whether graph edges are consistent and whether node attributes are similar. These two kinds of evidence contribute to a posterior probability for each candidate match, combining structural agreement with agreement in geometric description.

Node features are built from normalized histograms of pairwise geometric attributes. The method compares these histograms using Bhattacharyya distance, providing a measure of similarity between their distributions. Recognition then selects the database candidate with the highest posterior probability. This connects the feature comparison and graph structure to one probabilistic decision rule.

The authors demonstrate the method on a database of 2,500 line patterns extracted from real-world imagery. In that setting, it significantly outperforms several alternative algorithms. The result supports the usefulness of combining edge consistency with histogram-based node similarity for the reported recognition task. The contribution includes both a concrete geometric representation and a Bayesian way to use that representation when ranking candidate graph matches.
neurips-1998-graph-matching-for-shape-re.tldr: A Bayesian graph matcher combines edge consistency and geometric histogram similarity, outperforming alternatives on a database of 2,500 line patterns.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes calcium oscillations inside an insulin-secreting hamster cell under pharmacological stimulation. Intracellular calcium helps regulate cellular processes, and its signals can form complex patterns across both space and time. The authors use independent component analysis to investigate whether measured mixtures contain distinguishable independent temporal signals.

A fast fixed-point ICA algorithm performs blind source separation on five differently mixed input signals from the cell. The analysis identifies two significant independent components. One has an average oscillation period of 68 seconds. The other contains high-frequency activity with a broad power spectrum and considerable spectral density. These findings distinguish components with different temporal characteristics within the measured calcium dynamics.

The authors report agreement with a separate study of high-frequency calcium oscillations. The decomposition provides evidence about the structure of the recorded signals, but their biological function remains unresolved. The paper explicitly calls for further theoretical and experimental work to determine the functional impact of these independent signals on intracellular signaling. Its contribution is signal separation and characterization, with that functional question left open.
neurips-1998-independent-component-analy.tldr: ICA separates five calcium recordings into two significant components with distinct temporal behavior, while their functional roles remain unresolved.

paragraphs: The paper develops a hierarchical probabilistic model for real-valued data, motivated by tasks such as object and speech recognition. The authors argue that binary-unit belief networks are usually inadequate for these data and that independent component analysis has limited descriptive power. They begin with independent factor analysis, or IFA, which addresses some of ICA's limitations.

The hierarchy is constructed by cascading single-layer IFA models. Each level extracts real-valued latent variables that are nonlinear functions of its input, with highly adaptable functional forms. Passing these representations through successive levels produces a hierarchical distributed representation. The contribution is thus a way to build multiple levels of real-valued structure from the single-layer IFA model.

Exact maximum-likelihood learning for the resulting network is intractable. The authors derive a variational learning algorithm that instead maximizes a lower bound on likelihood. This supplies a tractable optimization target tied to the probabilistic model. The distinction matters: the algorithm optimizes the stated bound, while the richer multilayer representation makes direct exact likelihood optimization computationally unavailable.
neurips-1998-learning-a-hierarchical-bel.tldr: Cascaded independent factor analyzers learn hierarchical real-valued representations through a variational lower bound on likelihood.

paragraphs: The paper introduces an extension of expectation-maximization for learning hierarchies of mixture models. Such hierarchies organize data at multiple levels, with applications including data mining, machine vision, and information retrieval. The method builds upward from an existing level by clustering its mixture components to produce the components at the level above.

The efficiency comes from operating directly on mixture parameters. Constructing the next level does not require intermediate samples, so the information already contained in the fitted components drives the clustering. This gives the bottom-up procedure a specific computational advantage and makes the hierarchy an organization of model components as well as a representation of data.

The authors also use the method to reinterpret EM. Their analysis clarifies its relationship to non-parametric kernel-based estimation and provides explicit control over the bias–variance trade-off in EM estimates. It further offers insight into deterministic annealing methods used with EM to escape local likelihood minima. These connections make the contribution both an efficient hierarchical learning procedure and a framework for understanding related estimation and optimization behavior.
neurips-1998-learning-mixture-hierarchie.tldr: An EM extension efficiently builds mixture hierarchies by clustering component parameters and clarifies connections to kernel estimation and annealing.

paragraphs: MALCOM is a probabilistic model for sequences such as speech. It replaces the discrete hidden space and fixed finite-automaton architecture of a hidden Markov model with a continuous hidden space. Paths through this space must be smooth. The authors present this continuity constraint as a more realistic way to represent the speech production process within a compatible probabilistic recognition framework.

To assess whether the representation captures production information, the authors construct continuity maps for continuous speech from three speakers. They use paths inferred from speech acoustics to predict measured articulator data. On an independent test set used to train neither MALCOM nor the predictor, the median correlation between predictions from these paths and articulator measurements is 0.77.

Across speakers and articulators, correlations are only 0.02 to 0.15 below an analogous supervised method that uses articulator measurements as well as acoustics. These results support the presence of speech-production information in the acoustically learned representation. The evaluation concerns the relationship to articulator measurements, supplying evidence for the model's proposed hidden-space interpretation.
neurips-1998-maximum-likelihood-continui.tldr: MALCOM learns smooth continuous speech representations whose paths predict articulator measurements with a median test correlation of 0.77.

paragraphs: The paper studies how well two-layer feedforward networks approximate functions when built incrementally. The algorithms greedily add units, estimating the parameters of one unit at each stage. Each optimization therefore involves relatively few parameters, mitigating numerical difficulties that arise when optimizing a large fixed architecture through a high-dimensional nonlinear problem.

The authors establish upper bounds on approximation error for functions in a Sobolev class. This extends earlier convergence-rate results that applied to functions in certain convex hulls of function spaces. The bounds quantify the accuracy obtainable through the incremental procedure for the function class under study, giving theoretical support to a computationally simpler construction strategy.

Comparing these upper bounds with recently derived lower bounds shows that the greedy algorithms are nearly optimal in the analyzed setting. The claim concerns approximation performance relative to those bounds, with the function-class qualification remaining essential. Together with estimation-error results for greedy algorithms, the analysis makes a strong case for incremental network construction as an approach that combines manageable optimization steps with favorable theoretical accuracy.
neurips-1998-on-the-optimality-of-increm.tldr: Error bounds show that greedy unit-by-unit construction of two-layer networks is nearly optimal for the analyzed Sobolev function class.

paragraphs: The paper applies reinforcement learning to admission control in a telecommunications network. The objective combines earning revenue with maintaining a required quality of service. Admission decisions therefore have to account for both the value of accepting traffic and whether the resulting network behavior remains within the permitted operating conditions.

Quality of service is expressed as a constraint that forbids entry into certain states. This gives the problem a specific structure: revenue is optimized subject to a restriction on where the system may go. A successful policy must address both requirements together. The formulation makes acceptable network operation part of the decision problem itself, rather than treating revenue as the sole criterion.

The authors present a general solution to this multi-criteria problem and report significantly higher revenue than alternatives. The stated result indicates that their reinforcement learning approach can improve the economic objective while addressing the service constraint. Its contribution is the joint treatment of optimization and forbidden states in the admission-control setting, with revenue improvement reported for the alternatives examined.
neurips-1998-optimizing-admission-contro.tldr: A reinforcement learning approach improves admission-control revenue while handling quality-of-service constraints expressed as forbidden network states.

paragraphs: The paper examines why boosting can overfit noisy data despite its strong behavior in low-noise settings. The authors explain the problem through hard classification margins: boosting continues trying to enforce a strict separation even when observations include outliers. Giving those points too much weight can produce irregular fits and overfitting.

Their response is to introduce regularization through slack variables, allowing a soft margin. This permits controlled departures from the margin requirement instead of forcing every difficult observation to satisfy it. The paper proposes three algorithms: AdaBoostreg, a regularized linear-programming version of AdaBoost, and a regularized quadratic-programming version. All three bring this relaxation into the boosting framework.

Experiments demonstrate the usefulness of the proposed methods in comparison with support vector machines, which also provide soft-margin classification. The result supports regularization as a response to the outlier sensitivity described by the authors. The contribution is a family of concrete boosting variants that balance fitting the data against the pressure to enforce a hard margin in noisy classification problems.
neurips-1998-regularizing-adaboost-6637d.tldr: Three regularized AdaBoost variants introduce soft margins to address excessive outlier weighting and overfitting in noisy data.

paragraphs: The paper addresses a weakness of word-count-based text retrieval: sharing words does not by itself establish that a document is relevant to a query. A simple dot-product score measures overlap in terms, but the authors seek a representation that captures more of the structure connecting words within the document collection.

Their method constructs sparse representations from sets of highly related words. Documents and queries are described by their distances to these sets, and relevance is measured through shared clusters. This changes the unit of comparison from individual terms to groups of related terms. The approach is proposed as an alternative to linear dimensionality reduction for improving retrieval.

The authors report a significant improvement in retrieval performance together with efficient computation. They also identify properties shared with the optimal linear projection operator and with independent components of documents. These connections relate the representation to other ways of extracting underlying structure. The central contribution is a sparse, cluster-based description that makes word relationships part of the retrieval score.
neurips-1998-restructuring-sparse-high-d.tldr: Sparse representations based on related-word clusters significantly improve reported retrieval performance while remaining efficient to compute.

paragraphs: The paper develops improvements to parti-game, a reinforcement learning algorithm motivated by the difficulty of learning in high-dimensional problems. The authors describe the existing algorithm as promising for overcoming the curse of dimensionality. Their work builds on that promise by modifying the algorithm to improve its performance and robustness.

A second contribution concerns improving the solutions parti-game already finds. Standard path-improvement techniques can refine a solution locally, making changes in its immediate vicinity. The authors introduce an additional algorithm that instead attempts non-local improvements. This broadens the kind of revision considered, allowing the improvement process to look beyond nearby adjustments to the current solution.

The two contributions address different aspects of the method: the core modifications improve its operation, while the add-on targets further improvement of its solutions. The abstract describes the non-local procedure as an attempt to improve solutions, so its significance is the expanded search strategy rather than a stated guarantee of global optimality. Together, the changes extend parti-game's approach to difficult reinforcement learning problems.
neurips-1998-robust-efficient-globally-o.tldr: The paper improves parti-game's performance and robustness and adds a procedure that seeks non-local improvements to its solutions.

paragraphs: The paper extends support vector machines and linear programming machines to semiparametric modeling. Its motivation is a learning problem in which something is already known about the function being estimated, or in which the resulting model needs to be understandable. These priorities make the form of the model an important part of the learning task.

A semiparametric approach brings structured modeling choices together with flexibility in estimating a function. In the setting described by the authors, this offers a way to accommodate domain knowledge while retaining a learning algorithm's ability to fit data. The paper's methodological contribution is to make both of the named learning frameworks available for this type of model.

The authors also provide experimental results for the support vector machine extension. This gives empirical work for one of the two proposed extensions, alongside the broader algorithmic contribution. The paper matters as an expansion of the modeling choices available within these frameworks: prior understanding of the target function and concern for interpretability can motivate the model, rather than being separate from its formulation.
neurips-1998-semiparametric-support-vect.tldr: The paper extends support vector and linear programming machines to semiparametric models motivated by domain knowledge and interpretability.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how the timing of neuronal spikes can shape synaptic learning and ongoing neural activity. Its starting point is experimental evidence that a connection may strengthen or weaken depending on the relative timing of spikes in the neurons on either side of that connection. The temporal relationship therefore carries information relevant to the direction of learning.

The authors examine a Hebbian modification rule based on these observations. The rule leads to a stable state in which excitatory and inhibitory inputs to a neuron are balanced. In that state, the neuron fires irregularly. The result links a timing-dependent change at individual synapses to a broader pattern in the neuron's inputs and output.

This is relevant to the proposal that neurons in living organisms operate in such a balanced, irregular-firing mode. The learning rule supplies a mechanism that reaches a state with those properties in the described model. The finding connects synaptic adaptation with response variability, while the correspondence to neurons in vivo remains framed as a proposed operating regime.
neurips-1998-temporally-asymmetric-hebbi.tldr: A spike-timing-dependent Hebbian rule leads to balanced excitation and inhibition with stable but irregular neuronal firing.

paragraphs: The paper connects belief propagation and TAP in the task of decoding corrupted messages. It studies messages encoded by Sourlas's method, a special case of a Gallager error-correcting code. Encoded entries are products of K randomly selected message bits, making K a central feature of the decoding problem examined by the authors.

The authors show similarities between the two methods and compare the effectiveness of their solutions for different values of K. For unbiased patterns with K at least three, solutions may depend sensitively on the initial conditions. This means the starting point of the decoding procedure can matter in that setting; the abstract states this as a possibility rather than an unavoidable outcome.

Good approximations are generally obtained when K equals two and, for larger K, when the patterns are biased. Results are especially favorable when using Nishimori's temperature. These distinctions make the finding conditional on the encoding and pattern setting. The paper contributes both a relationship between two inference approaches and an account of circumstances associated with useful approximations or sensitivity to initialization.
neurips-1998-the-belief-in-tap-20d26dd83.tldr: Belief propagation and TAP behave similarly in Sourlas decoding, with approximation quality and initialization sensitivity depending on encoding and pattern conditions.

paragraphs: The paper introduces Sequential Minimal Optimization, or SMO, for training support vector machines. SVM training requires solving a potentially very large quadratic programming problem. SMO divides it into a sequence of the smallest possible quadratic subproblems, each of which has an analytical solution. This makes a numerical quadratic-programming library unnecessary.

The decomposition changes where computation is spent. Kernel evaluations dominate SMO's running time, so optimizing those evaluations can substantially accelerate training. The paper thus identifies both a way to simplify the optimization machinery and the main computational operation to target for further speed improvements. Its approach turns the large optimization problem into repeated manageable steps.

Reported comparisons show that the speed advantage depends strongly on the setting. SMO is 1.7 times as fast as PCG chunking on MNIST. For the UCI Adult dataset with linear SVMs, it can be 1,500 times faster. These results demonstrate substantial practical potential, with the largest gain attached to the specific dataset and model configuration stated by the authors.
neurips-1998-using-analytic-qp-and-spars.tldr: SMO speeds SVM training by solving minimal quadratic subproblems analytically, with reported gains ranging from 1.7-fold to as much as 1,500-fold.
